Theme

Nature & food

air noun

what we breathe

also fresh air, in the air, the open air, in the open air, a breath of air, atmosphere, the atmosphere

classical

Cic. N.D. 2.91
Plin. Ep. 5.6.5: semper āēr spīritū aliquō movētur

āēr, āëris m.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

air, the lower atmosphere

A Greek word long at home in Latin, as Cicero says; accusative āëra.

Other words

  • aura, aurae f. — a breath of air, a breeze; in poetry, the air

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 5.6.5: frequentius tamen aurās quam ventōs habet (Lewis & Short); Verg. A. 3.339: vēscitur aurā · Declension on Wiktionary

    (in hōc sēnsū vōx plērumque poētica: Lucr., Verg.)

  • sub dīvō — in the open air, under the open sky

    also used · classical · Cels. 1.2; Suet. Caes. 72; Hor. C. 2.3.23 (Lewis & Short s.v. dīvus); Traupman 136

Examples

  • terra … circumfūsa undique est hāc animālī spīrābilīque nātūrā, cui nōmen est āēr, Graecum illud quidem sed perceptum jam tamen ūsū ā nostrīs; trītum est enim prō Latīnō

    the earth is surrounded on every side by this living, breathable element called aer: a Greek word, but one our people have taken up by use, for it is worn smooth as if it were LatinCic. N.D. 2.91

  • aestātis mīra clēmentia: semper āēr spīritū aliquō movētur

    the summer is wonderfully mild: there is always a breath of air stirringPlin. Ep. 5.6.5

  • quid puer Ascanius? superatne et vēscitur aurā?

    and the boy Ascanius? Is he alive, does he still breathe the air?Verg. A. 3.339
